Week 2 · Research Ethics Study Guide

The Ethics of Paying Research Participants

Five readings, one question: when money meets risk, what makes research participation ethical? This guide integrates all five papers into a single narrative — from the foundations of human research, through the debate over payment, to two modern test cases: Phase I trials and human infection challenge studies.

5 papers digested 9 original figures, tables & boxes embedded Glossary + self-check questions Works offline — one file
🎯 How to use this guide

The papers are regrouped by concept, not by reading order. Part 1 gives you the foundations, Part 2 the central debate, Part 3 two real-world applications, Part 4 ties everything together. Use the sidebar to navigate; click any figure to zoom.

🧭 The one-sentence version

Payment is ethical when the research itself is ethical and payment is itemized by function — reimbursement, compensation, and incentive — each justified by fairness and calibrated with safeguards, so that both too much and too little payment raise ethical concerns.

⌨️ Features

Search box (sidebar) filters the whole guide · purple-highlighted terms are key vocabulary (hover them) · colored dots track which paper each section comes from · Self-check questions hide their answers until you click · Ctrl/Cmd+P prints cleanly.

The five papers at a glance

Stoops (2022)
Perspectives on Behavior Science · SQAB Tutorial

What it is: a methods-and-ethics primer on human behavioral pharmacology — controlled lab research that gives drugs to humans.

Why it matters here: it grounds the whole debate in how participants are actually used and paid (wage-payment model), and frames ethics with the Belmont principles.

Wong & Bernstein (2011)
Am J Med Sci 342(4) · Symposium

What it is: a provocatively titled argument that paying subjects for more-than-minimal-risk research is unethical — moral, logical, and pragmatic case, plus an original patient survey.

Why it matters here: it is the sharpest statement of the classic objections (undue influence, commodification, injustice) that the framework papers must answer.

Gelinas et al. (2018)
New England J Medicine 378:766–71 · Sounding Board

What it is: the field's consensus-forming framework — itemize payment into reimbursement, compensation, and incentive, each with its own justification.

Why it matters here: it supplies the conceptual toolkit (coercion vs. undue influence, mere vs. undue influence) every later paper builds on.

McManus et al. (2019)
J Law, Medicine & Ethics 47:323–33

What it is: a qualitative study of how Phase I healthy volunteers talk about adverse events — minimizing, denying, or re-attributing harm.

Why it matters here: it shows payment's downstream effects in practice: economically motivated participants narrate risk in self-protective ways, complicating consent.

Lynch et al. (2021)
Am J Bioethics 21(3):11–31 · Target article

What it is: a working-group analysis of payment for SARS-CoV-2 human infection challenge studies — the most extreme case of paid risk-taking.

Why it matters here: it stress-tests the Gelinas framework at the boundary (deliberate infection, confinement, no cure) and operationalizes it into a payment worksheet.

How they fit together
The reading order that isn't the publication order

Foundations (Stoops) → the objection (Wong & Bernstein) → the framework (Gelinas) → the stress tests (McManus, Lynch). The debate in Part 2 is the spine of the course week; Parts 3 shows the framework working — and straining — in practice.

Part 1 · Foundations

Human Behavioral Pharmacology — Where Paid Risk-Taking Begins

Before debating payment, understand the laboratory tradition that gave rise to it. Stoops (2022) explains how researchers give controlled doses of drugs to human volunteers — and how those volunteers are compensated.

1.1  What is human behavioral pharmacology?

Human behavioral pharmacology is the controlled study of the behavioral and pharmacological effects of centrally acting drugs — especially drugs of abuse — in humans. It has been practiced since at least the 1940s, with much early work done at the U.S. Public Health Service Addiction Research Center in Lexington, Kentucky — a history with its own ethical shadow: that early research was conducted with prisoners sent to the prison hospital because of their substance-use disorders. The center later became the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA).

Historical context — a precursor to modern research ethics

The Lexington studies are an example of the vulnerable-population research that the National Commission addressed in the 1970s, leading to restrictions on using prisoners in research. The field's history is inseparable from the ethics framework it now follows.

The field sits at a specific point on the translational spectrum — between preclinical work (in vitro, nonhuman animals) and clinical trials — and serves three purposes:

1 · Mechanisms

Determine basic biological, behavioral, and pharmacological mechanisms related to substance-use disorder.

2 · Abuse potential

Evaluate the abuse liability of novel compounds before they reach the market.

3 · Treatment screening

Screen putative substance-use-disorder treatments before advancement to expensive clinical trials.

It is now practiced at numerous institutions — including the University of Kentucky, Columbia, Brown, Johns Hopkins, Minnesota, VCU, and Chicago — and functions as a pipeline for developing and advancing novel medications.

Source: Stoops 2022, Introduction (pp. 1–2)

1.2  The classic methods — and their ethical stakes

Stoops organizes the field's toolkit into three classic measures (summarized in the paper's Table 1, embedded below), plus emerging novel methods.

Table · Stoops 2022
Table 1 — Summary of classic human behavioral pharmacology methods. The three classic measures differ in what they capture: self-administration measures willingness to take the drug (reinforcing effects); drug discrimination measures the drug's discriminative stimulus effects (what the subject perceives they took); and subjective-effects questionnaires capture self-reported interoceptive effects. Click to zoom.
① Drug self-administration — the objective measure of drug taking

Subjects first sample a dose of the drug under study, then are given opportunities to work to earn that dose again — from simple choice (a verbal indication, conceptually a fixed-ratio-1 schedule) to complex progressive-ratio schedules. Outcomes are expressed as a single variable: number of drug choices, or the break point.

Example designs: Foltin & Fischman (1992) let subjects sample smoked (0/25/50 mg) and intravenous (0/16/32 mg) cocaine, then make five choices between full sampled doses. Stoops et al. (2004) tested oral d-amphetamine (0/8/16/24 mg) and methylphenidate (0/16/32/48 mg) with subjects working for one-eighth portions of the dose across an eight-component progressive-ratio schedule. In both, active doses were self-administered more than placebo.

  • Concordance: most drugs that function as reinforcers in nonhuman animals do so in humans, and vice versa — drugs used recreationally generally function as reinforcers in the lab.
  • Clinical relevance: increasing an alternative reinforcer's magnitude or the response cost for the drug decreases intake — the logic behind contingency-management treatments.
  • Predictive validity: human self-administration is a "screen" for substance-use-disorder interventions with good predictive validity; preclinical models may have less.
② Drug discrimination — what the drug "feels like" objectively

Subjects sample a training drug (Drug A), learn to discriminate it from placebo (Not Drug A), and then allocate points between the options — points allocated correctly are exchangeable for money. The outcome is percent drug-appropriate responding. Two designs: substitution (test novel drugs against the training drug) and combination (test the training drug plus another drug).

Example: after subjects learned to discriminate 10 mg oral methamphetamine from placebo, Sevak et al. (2009) tested methamphetamine, d-amphetamine, and methylphenidate (all increased drug-appropriate responding) versus triazolam (did not) — demonstrating pharmacological selectivity. A follow-up showed aripiprazole attenuated methamphetamine-appropriate responding.

Notably, instructional control lets humans acquire discriminations much faster than animals — but drug discrimination is now less used in humans, because unlike self-administration it lacks a direct clinical correlate.

③ Subjective-effects questionnaires — the human-specific measure

Humans can verbally report their interoceptive drug effects — from direct questions ("How high is the drug making you feel right now?") to craving measures, the Profile of Mood States, and the Addiction Research Center Inventory. Responses are always quantified (100-unit visual analog scale, Likert scales, composite scores) and analyzed as a time course, peak effect, or area under the curve.

Example: Walsh et al. (1995) compared oral methadone (a full μ-opioid agonist — dose-related increases in subjective effects) with sublingual buprenorphine (a partial agonist — it did not produce them), showing how efficacy and potency shape the subjective response.

Subjective measures are the simplest and most common classic measure, provide key abuse-liability data to regulatory agencies, but co-vary with — without being identical to — self-administration and discrimination outcomes; using them in concert gives the most thorough assessment.

Novel methods — extending the toolkit

Drug purchase tasks (behavioral economics): hypothetical purchases of a drug across a range of prices yield demand parameters — intensity, elasticity, breakpoint, maximum expenditure. Being evaluated as a substitute for self-administration outcomes, valuable for screening interventions in people who cannot safely be administered drugs.

Attentional bias: the disproportionate allocation of attention to drug cues vs. neutral cues, measured by eye tracking or visual-probe tasks. People who use drugs display it routinely; cocaine pharmacotherapies (methylphenidate, N-acetylcysteine) can attenuate it.

Source: Stoops 2022, Methods (pp. 3–8)
Take-home — Methods

The three classic measures provide complementary windows on drug effects: whether the drug maintains behavior (self-administration), what it resembles (discrimination), and how it feels (subjective effects). Ethically, all three involve administering drugs of abuse to humans — which is precisely why the design and ethics scaffolding that follows matters.

1.3  Design considerations — the practical scaffolding

Subject selection

Subjects should have experience with the drug and route under study (e.g., a THC-positive urine screen for cannabis studies). Subjects should not be exposed to a more invasive route than they have experience with — with careful exceptions. Drug-naïve subjects are enrolled only in vulnerability research, using the least invasive route, with follow-up. Teams must screen mental and physical health to rule out contraindications.

Outcome selection

Because these studies are a substantial investment per subject, multiple outcomes are common — chosen by hypotheses but constrained by the drug's time course, timeline, cost, and subject burden.

Dose range & route

Humans get 2- to 10-fold dose ranges (not the log-scale ranges used in animals), chosen from safety data and FDA guidelines. Route depends on the question and facility medical capacity — parenteral routes require hospital-grade supervision. An IND application to the FDA is needed if: (1) dosing above the recommended daily maximum, (2) a non-approved route, (3) a non-approved drug, (4) data will support an FDA indication, or (5) a Schedule I drug is tested.

Comparator drugs

An active negative control distinguishes general drug effects from drug-class-specific effects; for abuse-liability studies, the comparator should be a well-characterized drug with a similar indication or receptor system.

Placebo control & blinding

Because expectancy effects influence drug response, double-blind placebo control is the most desirable design; placebos should physically mimic active doses; a double-dummy approach covers multi-route or multi-time designs. Note the ethical tension: blinding obstructs fully informed consent — addressed in §1.4.

Within- vs. between-subjects

Within-subjects designs minimize subjects and maximize power (each subject is their own control) but risk attrition and carry-over effects; between-subjects designs require careful group matching.

Key concept — Subject Payment (the bridge to this week's theme)

Participation requires a substantive time commitment — screening can take several multi-hour visits, and sessions run 4–8 hours. It is therefore customary to compensate subjects for their time. Approaches include a wage-payment model or reimbursement. Stoops's lab matches payments to the approximate living wage and structures a completion bonus to encourage finishing.

On the worry that paying people with substance-use disorders will increase drug use: evidence shows subjects may spend some payments on drugs but their drug-use behavior does not change after study participation (Festinger & Dugosh 2012; Thurstone et al. 2010). The paternalistic objection thus fails empirically — a point of direct contact with the payment debate in Part 2.

Source: Stoops 2022, Design Considerations (pp. 9–12)

1.4  Ethics — the Belmont principles in the human laboratory

Stoops grounds the field's ethics in the three Belmont principles. This is the conceptual foundation the rest of the week's readings assume.

Beneficence

Research must produce benefit (subject, society, or both) and risks must not outweigh benefits. Benefits to subjects: rigorous medical screening and remuneration (though not all IRBs count payment as a benefit). Risk mitigation: comfortable environment near physician offices, rescue medication, conservative dosing-termination criteria. Societal benefit example: behavioral-pharmacology data showing crack and powder cocaine are pharmacologically similar informed the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 — challenging racially biased sentencing minimums.

Respect for persons

Autonomy is protected through informed consent as an ongoing process — a signature on a document is not sufficient. Key practices: (1) verify capacity to consent (study quizzes, teach-back methods, mental-status screening); (2) adequate time to read and process; (3) opportunity to discuss with the PI. Because blinding threatens consent, Stoops's lab discloses the full list of possible drugs/doses/routes plus known side effects, with an advisory that subjects won't know which they receive on a given day — and offers full debriefing afterward.

Justice

Populations who benefit from research should participate in it, and burdens should be distributed across them. Practices: (1) think broadly about populations affected by the condition; (2) use the most open inclusion/exclusion criteria safety allows; (3) plan recruitment of diverse populations matching the affected demographics; (4) partner with surrounding communities. This is the hardest principle here — treatment-seekers and higher-risk individuals are excluded though they would benefit most.

Take-home — Balancing the principles

No single Belmont principle is paramount; teams must balance them against one another while also managing safety. The tension is structural: excluding treatment-seekers protects them (beneficence) but denies participation to those who might benefit most (justice). The field's standards evolve — e.g., current debates about enrolling treatment-seeking individuals in alcohol-administration research.

Source: Stoops 2022, Ethics (pp. 12–15)
Part 2 · The Payment Debate

Should Participants Be Paid at All?

Two papers in direct opposition: Wong & Bernstein (2011) argue payment for more-than-minimal-risk research is unethical, period. Gelinas et al. (2018) respond — not by citing Wong directly, but by dismantling the conceptual foundations the objection rests on and replacing them with a practical framework.

2.1  The case against payment — Wong & Bernstein (2011)

Wong & Bernstein address payment above and beyond reimbursement of costs, in studies with more than minimal risk. Their claim: payment is ethically unacceptable, and not paying is "the only ethical option currently available." They build the argument on three legs — moral, logical, and pragmatic.

Leg 1 — The moral argument: undue influence & commodification
  • Payment is a "unique influence." A participant weighing a paid study balances x% probability of health risk against a 100% guaranteed payment. Because payment is the only certain outcome, it biases the decision toward participation — it is not "just one of many influences." Even with perfect informed consent (probably unattainable), this asymmetry persists.
  • Commodification of health. Following Chambers, payment transforms participants' health into a commodity — and this occurs whether participation is framed as a gift or a job. "Health cannot be measured in monetary currency."
  • Beyond the utilitarian view. Kuczewski worried payment invites public scorn and undermines the medical profession. The authors push further: payment is wrong in and of itself (a deontological claim), because commodifying human health is fundamentally wrong.
Evidence — the patient survey

A focused qualitative study sampled 190 neurosurgery clinic patients (March–September 2010, convenience sampling) with a scenario: $1,500 up-front to join a hypothetical randomized controlled trial relevant to the patient's condition. Results:

Opinion on the $1,500 paymentn%Typical reasoning
Unethical10756%Payment is an undue influence, or wrongfully commodifies clinical research
Ethical7037%Payment justly compensates any potential risks incurred
Could not comment137%—

Caveats the authors note: the sample was mostly middle-class Canadian patients with access to "free" health care — so results may not generalize to (say) the United States.

Leg 2 — The logical argument: financial need distorts the risk calculus

From two "reasonable assumptions": (1) increased risk → decreased willingness to participate, and (2) more financial need → increased willingness to participate. Combining them on a graph (Figure 1, below) shows that people with more financial need cross the participation threshold at higher risk levels. Payment therefore unjustly influences poorer patients to accept harmful risks — supported by Casarett et al., who found those reporting they would be influenced by $500 had lower incomes. The authors extend the concern to clinical trials in the developing world, where the most economically vulnerable may be financially induced, and research benefits often do not fairly accrue to participants.

Figure 1 · Wong & Bernstein 2011
FIGURE 1 — The relationship between risks, financial need, and willingness to participate in a study. Willingness (y-axis) falls as risk (x-axis) rises. The dashed line (more financial need) sits above the solid line (less financial need): at any given level of risk, the financially needy are more willing to participate. Where the curves cross the "threshold" of willingness, the financially needy cross it at a higher level of risk — the graphical core of the unjust-influence argument. (The authors note the graph is a philosophical construct, not measured data.)
Leg 3 — The pragmatic argument: regulation models fail

Previous proposals to standardize payment — a wage-payment model (Dickert & Grady), an employer-dependent reimbursement model (Stones & McMillan), and a labor contract (Lemmens & Elliott) — are criticized on two grounds: they do not resolve the ethical problems (commodification and unjust influence remain), and they are not feasible (unclear how they could be universally integrated and IRB-monitored). Moreover, any payment limit would be arbitrary: Czarny et al. found participants' estimates of fair payment vary widely, and Weise et al. found IRBs approve widely ranging minimal and maximal payments. Since willingness tracks payment generosity (several studies), payment genuinely influences participation.

The conclusion — and why it matters

"A policy of not paying research subjects for participation in studies with more than minimal risks should be adopted." This is the strongest version of the classic objection. Note the position's structure: it concedes reimbursement for costs and payment for minimal-risk studies, and attacks only payment beyond that — but attacks it absolutely. The framework papers of 2018–2021 are, in effect, a systematic reply.

Source: Wong & Bernstein 2011, Am J Med Sci 342(4):294–296

2.2  The framework answer — Gelinas et al. (2018)

Writing in NEJM's Sounding Board, Gelinas, Largent, Cohen, Kornetsky, Bierer, and Lynch — informed by a multi-stakeholder working group of ethicists, IRB members, investigators, regulators, participants, and industry representatives — set out to end the "substantial disagreement and confusion" over what makes a payment "excessive." Their framework has become the field's common language.

Step 1 — Fix the definitions
Coercion

A situation involving a threat to harm someone or violate a person's rights. Offers of payment are offers, not threats — by definition, payment cannot coerce.

Undue influence

An offer of something desirable that influences decision making in inappropriate ways — when the offer's attractiveness causes participants to unreasonably discount or fail to appreciate risks, threatening the validity of consent.

These definitions trace to the Belmont Report and OHRP guidance — and they reframe the entire debate: the regulatory question is only about undue influence. Crucially, there is also "mere" influence, which is unproblematic: just as an employer may offer a higher salary to attract a candidate, "payment may appropriately influence the decision to participate in IRB-approved research." OHRP itself states that "compensation may be an acceptable motive for agreeing to participate in research."

Step 2 — Take the concerns seriously, then size them
ConcernThe worryThe framework's response
Undermining valid consent Payment may distort judgment of risks, invalidating consent. No bright line exists — the line differs per person. Limited data suggest payment may actually increase caution and risk perception. Rather than restricting payment, IRBs should safeguard consent directly (comprehension assessments), especially as amounts and risks rise.
Inducing deception Participants might deceive investigators about eligibility (a safety and integrity risk). Some research (e.g., phase 1 with healthy volunteers) is more susceptible; assess case-by-case — overbroad to restrict payment in all cases.
Unfair distribution of burdens Payment may disproportionately attract lower-SES participants. Offering less because participants are poor would exacerbate economic injustice. Seek corrective measures: wider recruitment strategies, fair distribution of risks and benefits — fair payment per the framework.

Also note: IRBs must determine that the research offer itself is reasonable without counting payment as a benefit — and IRB approval, while no substitute for valid consent, lowers the stakes of consent deficiencies by ensuring enrollment could not be characterized as unreasonable.

Step 3 — The framework: itemize payment by function

The core move: rather than asking "is the total too high?", ask what is each dollar for. Three categories, each with its own justification and concerns:

Reimbursement

For: out-of-pocket expenses (travel, parking, meals, accommodation, childcare).
Justification: restores participants to their financial baseline — "participants should not have to pay for making a contribution to the social good of research" (CIOMS).
Key property: no net benefit → cannot be unduly influential (FDA confirmed for travel costs, Jan 2018).
Ethical status: the default expectation, though not strictly obligatory (altruism, overlapping medical visits, or direct medical benefit can justify proceeding without it — but investigators must justify that to the IRB).

Compensation

For: time, burdens, and contributions.
Justification: fairness — research participation is equated with employment; avoiding exploitation requires adequately recompensing people for efforts contributing to socially valuable activities.
Key rules: rates should be uniform across participants (equal pay for equal "work") and not based on individual earning potential.
On risk: OHRP permits compensating for risk; CIOMS says compensation should not be based on risks. The framework's resolution: fairness is better achieved by compensating actual harms (via insurance) than paying for the possibility of harm — when harms materialize, compensation is required as a matter of justice.

Incentive

For: payment beyond what reimbursement and compensation justify.
Justification: improving recruitment and retention — studies that miss targets are underpowered or terminated, exposing participants to risk with limited offsetting social benefit.
Key property: the most controversial category, but regulatory guidance recognizes incentives as legitimate in principle.
Ethical status: appropriate to encourage enrollment in studies IRBs have approved as socially valuable and reasonable — higher offers help achieve that.

The operational guidance — Boxes 1 and 2

The paper translates the framework into checklists for the two audiences who set and review payment offers:

Box 1 · Gelinas et al. 2018 (NEJM)
Box 1 — Considerations for Investigators Proposing Payment Offers. Itemize payments by category with justification; treat reimbursement and compensation as the priority before assessing incentives; consult the IRB on reasonable expenses; justify compensation rates by analogy to nonresearch employment; offer incentives only beyond what reimbursement and compensation justify; consider insurance options for research-related injury; and increase consent safeguards as payment amounts increase.
Box 2 · Gelinas et al. 2018 (NEJM)
Box 2 — Considerations for IRBs Reviewing Payment Offers. Recognize the mere/undue influence distinction — payment can be an acceptable motivation; consider whether comprehension mechanisms would address distortion concerns rather than limiting payment; ensure payment concerns don't mask underlying discomfort with the risk–benefit ratio; recognize the positive ethical reasons for payment (fairness, trial completion → generalizable knowledge); require itemized payment categories; benchmark compensation to fair wages for similarly burdensome nonresearch work; and permit recruitment incentives when more than fair reimbursement and compensation is desired.
Take-home — The framework

Payments in all three categories "can be ethically acceptable, and indeed desirable." The framework's power is diagnostic: it replaces the vague question "is $X too much?" with the structured question "is each component of $X justified by its function?" — and it makes visible that low payment raises ethical concerns too (unfairness, inadequate recruitment, underpowered trials).

Source: Gelinas et al. 2018, N Engl J Med 378:766–771

2.3  The debate, head-to-head

QuestionWong & Bernstein (2011)Gelinas et al. (2018)
Can payment coerce?Payment "may not strictly conform to the definition of coercion" but is a unique — and uniquely certain — influence.By definition, no: coercion is a threat; payment is an offer. Only undue influence is ever in play.
Is payment inherently wrongful?Yes — it commodifies human health, which is "fundamentally wrong" (deontological claim).No — payment serves legitimate functions (fairness, recruitment); the employment analogy treats compensation for burdens as required fairness, not corruption.
Effect on the poorPayment unjustly influences the financially needy to accept higher risk (Figure 1 logic). Solution: don't pay.Withholding payment to "protect" the poor exacerbates economic injustice. Solution: fair payment + consent safeguards + wider recruitment.
What about high offers?Any limit would be arbitrary; high payment infinitely increases willingness — so eliminate payment.High offers are acceptable if each component is justified; concerns about "excessive" payment often mask deeper discomfort with the risk–benefit ratio, which should be addressed directly.
What about low/no payment?Not a concern — non-payment is the ethical baseline.Low payment raises significant ethical concerns: unfairness, exploitation of those without alternatives, inadequate recruitment, underpowered trials that waste participants' exposure to risk.
Evidence baseSingle-site patient survey (n=190) + conceptual argument.Multi-stakeholder working group; regulatory analysis (OHRP, FDA, CIOMS); empirical literature on payment effects.
Study tip — How to argue this on an exam

Be precise with the locus of disagreement. Wong & Bernstein treat payment as a single undifferentiated quantity whose size is the problem. Gelinas decompose it into functions — reimbursement, compensation, incentive — each with its own justification. Once decomposed, "don't pay" resolves into three separate claims ("don't refund expenses," "don't compensate time," "don't incentivize enrollment"), each of which the framework answers with a fairness argument. The debate also turns on the coercion vs. undue influence distinction: if payment is an offer rather than a threat, the strongest form of the objection ("payment coerces") fails by definition, and the argument must shift to when offers become undue — a question the framework answers with safeguards rather than prohibition.

Part 3 · Payment in Practice — Two Stress Tests

Phase I Trials and Human Infection Challenge Studies

The framework meets reality. McManus et al. show what paid risk-taking looks like from inside a Phase I trial; Lynch et al. apply the framework to the most extreme case — deliberately infecting healthy volunteers with SARS-CoV-2.

3.1  Appraising harm in Phase I trials — McManus et al. (2019)

Phase I trials test the safety and tolerability of investigational drugs in healthy volunteers. They occupy a distinctive ethical position: documenting and measuring harm is their primary purpose, and their participants are typically enrolled for the financial compensation — about $100–300 per day, with lengthy studies offering several thousand dollars, strikingly high compared to later-phase trials. Scholars have worried this acts as an undue inducement leading participants to accept risks they would otherwise reject — and to enroll serially.

Key definition — Adverse event (AE)

An AE is any physiological sign, symptom, or medical event experienced by a participant during a trial — causation is immaterial. Only after the trial ends do investigators and the sponsor adjudicate which AEs were likely caused by the drug ("side effects"); the rest are discounted as unrelated — often disappearing from reported results, "though not necessarily from the view of any participant." Meta-analyses suggest Phase I trials are relatively safe, but AEs are very common — one study found 65% of participants had at least one per trial, mostly minor and temporary (headaches, GI changes). Rarely, volunteers have died or suffered serious injuries.

The study

Semi-structured interviews (conducted 2014, one year after enrollment) with 131 healthy volunteers recruited from seven U.S. Phase I research clinics in 2013 — 90% of those the team successfully followed up. Interviews probed participants' own and others' AE experiences, their perception of AE frequency, and their beliefs about why AEs occur. Transcripts were coded in Dedoose; excerpts coded "Adverse Events/Side Effects" were analyzed.

Table 1 · McManus et al. 2019
Table 1 — Demographics of Study Participants (N = 131). The profile of the U.S. healthy-volunteer workforce: 75.6% men; 65.6% racial/ethnic minorities; 81% over age 30; only ~36% employed full-time; 84% reporting household income under $50,000; and 37.4% having participated in more than 10 Phase I trials. This is the population whose consent the payment debate is about — economically constrained, experienced, and serially enrolled.
The central finding

With little exception, participants minimized, denied, or re-attributed the cause of AEs — for events they experienced and events they witnessed in others — thereby rejecting the notion that a drug-related harm occurred. The authors identify three narrative strategies, shaped by the trial environment and participants' economic motivation:

StrategyHow it worksIllustrative case from the paper
① AEs as insignificant Bodily changes are real but trivial — compared against worse risks listed in consent forms, worse AEs of fellow participants (witnessed during confinement), or offset by the attentiveness of monitoring staff and the discharge health check. Alison dismissed fevers because she "didn't have any of the extreme side effects that were possible." Paolo — a serial participant with an estimated 26 trials over a decade — reasoned "nothing happens to us, and we're still healthy": his definition of harm rested on his continued ability to qualify as a healthy volunteer.
② AEs as imagined or fabricated The bodily change wasn't real at all — imagined (expectation effects in the "state of waiting" that confinement creates), psychosomatic, or fabricated by other participants (who supposedly exaggerate symptoms to leave early with full payment). Lindsay questioned her own nausea: "I think it's because I overthink it." Bruce declared "it's all psychosomatic" and imagined himself getting the placebo. Travis, with two decades of participation, suspected complainers of trying to "weasel out" of studies under policies paying full compensation for safety withdrawal.
③ AEs as distressing but not drug-caused The symptom was real and painful — but attributed to the clinic environment, study restrictions (e.g., caffeine withdrawal), or other participants' rule-breaking (lying to qualify, study-hopping), never the study drug. Jennifer couldn't tell whether her back pain came from the medication or "the hospital beds were terrible." Steve got headaches "in almost every study" but blamed caffeine withdrawal — while explicitly acknowledging the consent form lists headaches as a potential side effect. Everett witnessed a code blue and explained it by guessed illicit drug use and study-hopping — "without ever speculating that it could be a direct result of the study drug."

A secondhand account of the 2006 London (TGN1412/theralizumab) immunotherapy disaster was likewise distorted — Tammy "remembered" that participants died because they'd gone straight from one study to another, when in fact no one died (though some suffered life-threatening cytokine-storm reactions and permanent disfigurement) and post-trial investigations confirmed an unforeseen drug reaction, not participant misconduct.

The exception that proves the rule — Timothy

One participant did interpret his AE as a drug-related harm: Timothy, financially stable (household income over $100,000), lost significant weight and passed out at work during his first and only trial. He had no doubt the drug caused it — "it really made me sick… had I known those side effects would have happened to me, I would not have done the study" — and refused further participation. The authors' point: acknowledging harm requires admitting you knowingly exposed yourself to it, which is psychologically compatible with continued enrollment only if you can afford to stop — as Timothy could, unlike the serial participants who denied harm.

Take-home — Why this matters for the payment debate

Participants' narratives maintain the safety of Phase I trials and the ethics of testing drugs on healthy people — denial is "not only a self-serving narrative that allows them to continue to enroll," it "buttresses the research enterprise by maintaining a pool of willing participants." The ethical consequences run downstream: (1) it raises questions about whether informed consent can communicate risk when actual participants deny that risks translate into bodily harms; (2) participants disinclined to report bodily changes undermine the AE-monitoring that is the whole point of Phase I research — "flawed accountings of harm potentially jeopardize both the protection of research participants and the trustworthiness of trial results." The authors' proposal: return results to participants — telling serial enrollees how their past AEs were classified would sensitize them to study risks and make consent more meaningful.

Connection — Where this hits Part 2

McManus's participants are the empirical shadow of the figures in Wong & Bernstein's Figure 1: economically constrained people whose willingness to accept risk is entangled with financial need. The framework response (Gelinas, Lynch) is not to remove payment but to strengthen consent safeguards and comprehension assessment — precisely the interventions this study's findings call into question. Lynch et al. cite McManus & Fisher directly on payment-induced deception about adverse events — the risk that paid participants minimize or hide AEs to stay in studies and get paid.

Source: McManus, Davis, Forcier & Fisher 2019, J Law Med Ethics 47:323–333

3.2  Ethical payment in human infection challenge studies — Lynch et al. (2021)

Convened at the behest of 1Day Sooner (the organization advocating SARS-CoV-2 challenge trials), a multidisciplinary working group — HICS researchers, prospective participants, ethicists, attorneys, and economists — produced 52 recommendations on ethical payment (Lynch et al. 2020). The journal article distills the analysis. Human infection challenge studies (HICS) deliberately infect healthy participants with a pathogen — here, SARS-CoV-2, for which no proven cure existed at the time.

The central question: do HICS need their own payment framework?

The working group's answer — no — is argued systematically. Four candidate reasons for a special framework, each examined and rejected:

Candidate reasonThe concernWhy it doesn't require a new framework
Public trust Deliberately infecting people is uniquely disconcerting; payment missteps could damage trust in the whole research enterprise. Trust concerns cut both ways — UK data showed the public views payment as critically important in HICS, so low payment could also breed distrust. The basic framework "can serve an important role in responding to distrust" by explaining how and why offers are justified.
Risk level HICS are uniquely risky — you cannot withdraw from an infection once it takes hold. A Phase 1 toxicity study of a novel chemical entity can entail greater uncertainty and risk — yet payment there is routine. Safeguards (careful participant selection) can keep mortality risks low; risk is relevant to the ethical acceptability of the research, not to the structure of payment analysis.
Social value HICS could save millions of lives — Anomaly & Savulescu argue it may be appropriate to pay "any amount." The basic framework already highlights the ethical importance of using payment to achieve adequate recruitment and retention — the social-value claim is within the framework, not outside it.
Financial susceptibility Perhaps HICS participants are uniquely vulnerable to being swayed by money. Healthy participants generally have mixed motivations (money necessary but not sufficient; altruism, curiosity, thrill-seeking), and perceived risk — not payment — is the ultimate deciding factor. Data from HICS participants replicate this; prospective SARS-CoV-2 participants emphasized altruism. Notably, a majority of non-participants wouldn't join even if payment were doubled, and most who would consider it wouldn't if both risks and compensation were doubled — payments are resistible.
An important nuance

The group notes that the zeal of altruistically motivated participants may itself call for consent protections "typically associated with offers of payment" — to ensure volunteers have realistic expectations of the study's impact on the pandemic. Enthusiasm can distort judgment as surely as money can.

The "payment funnel" — from concept to dollar amount

The paper's methodological contribution is the payment funnel: the basic framework (from Gelinas et al. 2018) is the broad end, narrowing through increasingly specific factors until a defensible dollar figure emerges for a particular study. Table 1 (below) maps the whole funnel.

Table 1 · Lynch et al. 2021
Table 1 — The payment "funnel": factors relevant to ethical payment for participation in human infection challenge studies. Column 1 is the basic framework (note that compensation for harm appears as its own row); column 2 adds considerations relevant to all clinical research (direct medical benefit, early withdrawal, study location, study budget, participant perspectives); column 3 adds the factors especially salient for HICS (isolation and confinement, anticipated discomfort, risk of lasting harm, participant motivations, plus diversity, stigma, ethics review capacity, and public trust). Click to zoom — every cell is exam-relevant.

The framework's three categories, applied to HICS:

Reimbursement

Out-of-pocket expenses (travel, meals, dependent care) — offered "as a matter of fairness to avoid participants having to pay in order to contribute to socially valuable research." Raises no ethical concerns because it entails no net benefit; it also removes financial barriers, broadening the participant pool.

Compensation

For time, burden, and inconvenience — the same fairness justification as reimbursement. Fairness does not demand opportunity-cost-based pay (don't pay lawyers $400/hr and baristas $15); it demands equal pay for equal work. Because fair compensation may exceed participants' opportunity costs, undue influence becomes possible — but ethics approval limits the concern, and "the potential for unfairness through insufficient compensation is of greater concern" than the challenges of higher payment.

Incentives

Paid as needed to address recruitment/retention shortfalls. They carry the highest potential for undue influence — but inadequate recruitment has its own ethical costs (participants exposed to risk in studies that fail to answer their questions). On balance, incentives are justifiable in socially valuable, ethical research. The unjust-inducement worry (that offers disproportionately appeal to the worse-off) should be solved by encouraging wider participation across economic groups — never by paying less.

Key distinction — Compensation for harm

Compensation for significant research-related harms should be guaranteed through no-fault insurance covering short- and long-term medical costs, lost wages, pain and suffering, and death. Its persistent absence from U.S. regulation is "a major ethical concern." Because it is paid only if harm materializes, it is not a net benefit and raises no undue-influence concerns — and since assuming a risk that never materializes is not a loss, fairness does not demand that risk itself be compensated (though risk-based payments may be acceptable under other rationales). This is the analytic core the framework adds to Wong & Bernstein's fixed-pie framing.

The "further specifying" factors from Table 1's middle column, in brief:

  • Direct medical benefit — cannot justify reducing reimbursement/compensation; benefits are incommensurate with financial impacts, and justice demands fair distribution of benefits as well as burdens.
  • Early withdrawal or termination — prorate reimbursement and compensation; harms are compensated in full regardless; completion bonuses are acceptable when needed, limited to studies offering fair reimbursement/compensation, and participants terminated for unreasonable risk deserve any promised bonus since they completed their commitment.
  • Study location — comply with local requirements; use local minimum wage as a benchmark (possibly with multiples); consider competing studies at the site.
  • Economic vulnerability — sites and participants should not be selected for economic vulnerability; but withholding or reducing payment is not the remedy — it "aggravates a bad situation and is unfair." Focus on fairness and consent supports.
  • Study budget — reimbursement and compensation are the ethical default (deviation requires justification); compensation for harm is an absolute ethical requirement (like employers financing workers' compensation); incentives are the most discretionary — but if recruitment goals will only be met with incentives, proceeding without them is ethically problematic.
  • Participant perspectives — participants may face costs and burdens researchers are unaware of; certain payment types or cultural considerations may matter to motivation.
The HICS-specific factors — what makes challenge studies different

① Participant isolation and confinement. To prevent participants acquiring infection in the community (or spreading it), confinement may last several weeks and require social distancing even from other participants — a significant psychological burden. Reimbursement should cover the full duration; compensation should reflect the heightened burden; incentives and completion bonuses may become necessary as confinement lengthens. Consent supports should include test periods of confinement and involvement of prior HICS participants in the consent process.

② Anticipated discomfort. Participants can expect at least some illness — though for SARS-CoV-2, many infections are asymptomatic or mild. Payment should compensate for anticipated median discomfort, not actual discomfort — avoiding incentives to exaggerate or fabricate symptoms (the Phase I deception problem from McManus, appearing again at the protocol level).

③ Risk of lasting harm. Low in traditional HICS (treatable, self-limiting infections); for riskier HICS like SARS-CoV-2, comprehensive no-fault insurance is essential — "under no circumstances should such research be allowed to proceed without this guarantee." Heightened risk should not impede greater payment so long as the research is ethical and undue-influence safeguards are in place.

④ Participant motivations. If altruism predominates (as likely in a pandemic), incentives are probably unnecessary — but altruism must not rest on mistaken beliefs about the research's impact. Fair reimbursement and compensation remain important even for altruistic participants. Some prospective participants anticipated benefit from controlled infection — but since precautions make viral exposure avoidable, challenge exposure is difficult to characterize as a benefit.

Plus three more from Table 1's third column: Diverse recruitment — HICS's small size limits generalizability, so demographic diversity is less scientifically impactful than in other research; burdens should not be disproportionately concentrated on the disadvantaged; financial incentives aimed at specific communities could exacerbate worries about being "used as a guinea pig" — reduce financial barriers and emphasize fair compensation instead. Stigma — some HICS participants report negative responses or keep participation secret; stigma is insufficient reason to reduce fair payment; the better response is public understanding (and SARS-CoV-2 participants were characterized as "heroic"). Independent ethical approval — use review boards experienced with the design; the authors endorse specially constituted "Comprehensive Ethics Review Committees" for research with contentious risk and highly contingent social value.

What do challenge studies actually pay? — Table 2

Reviewing HICS registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (2015–2020), the authors could locate payment information for only 18 of 109 hits — itself evidence of a "problematic lack of transparency about payment practices." Table 2 (below) compiles what they found: substantial variability, most payment described as compensation for time, no study describing incentives as such, and harm compensation often not explicitly guaranteed. A survey by Grimwade et al. similarly found payments from £0 to £3,393 (≈ $0–$4,388) with hourly rates from £0 to £30 (≈ $0–$38.80) — and most investigators admitted they simply copied previous studies' amounts. The warning: using current payments as benchmarks "may result in merely replicating payments that are unnecessarily and inappropriately low."

Table 2 · Lynch et al. 2021
Table 2 — Payment in selected Human Infection Challenge Studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2015–2020, plus investigator contacts). Each row is one study: model organism (N. americanus hookworm, influenza, Plasmodium falciparum/vivax, RSV, Streptococcus, Salmonella, ETEC, dengue, BCG…), sponsor type, in/outpatient status, durations, and the payment breakdown — travel, accommodation, work time, screening, clinic time, receipt of the investigational product, receipt of the challenge agent, blood draws, inpatient/quarantine phase, additional procedures, completion bonuses, and insurance. Maximum totals ranged from $386 to $8,938. Click to zoom — the footnotes detail per-study payment structures.
The operational deliverable — the payment worksheet (Tables 3A & 3B)

The funnel's final step is a worksheet translating the framework into a systematic process for setting dollar amounts. Crucially, it is not a formula: "it invites reflection on relevant factors and benchmarks, implicitly acknowledging that there can be a range of reasonable payment amounts for any given study." The worksheet consists of two tables, deliberately separated.

Table 3A · Lynch et al. 2021
Table 3A — SARS-CoV-2 HICS payment worksheet (part 1). For each payment type — reimbursement, compensation, incentive — the worksheet tracks the goal (full coverage of reasonable expenses / fair payment for time and burden / encouraging enrollment and retention), variability (reimbursement varies per participant by incurred expenses; compensation is uniform across participants at the same site; incentives aim for uniformity), coverage (prorate for early withdrawal; completion bonuses only for completers), the factors to consider (from transportation and meals to confinement intensity, boredom, and "potential for payment-induced deception"), the relevant benchmarks (government reimbursement rates, minimum wage, pay scales of analogous occupations like firefighting, "time and a half" differentials, hazard pay like combat pay), and columns for proposed amounts, payment range, and the explanation offered to ethics review. Click to zoom.
Table 3B · Lynch et al. 2021
Table 3B — SARS-CoV-2 HICS: compensation for harm (part 2). The second worksheet table handles compensation for harm — injury (comprehensive medical and disability care, short and long term; free care vs. payment for care; national health system coverage — "do not rely on participants' private health insurance"), lost work (reduction in earning capacity within bounds; extent of lost ability to work), and death (lump sum; age; average lifespan). It is separated from Table 3A so harm compensation is never folded into calculations of expected total payment — harm is provided "if and only if harm materializes." U.S. benchmarks include workers' compensation, Social Security Disability Insurance, and the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. Click to zoom.
Take-home — Lynch et al.

The basic framework "divides payment into three categories — reimbursement, compensation, and incentive — and emphasizes the importance of fairness and adequate recruitment and retention." High offers "can be ethically appropriate," and low payment also raises significant ethical concerns. Because HICS involve lengthy confinement, anticipated discomfort, lasting-harm risk, and distinctive motivations, HICS "will likely be on the high end of the payment spectrum" — and researchers should be expected to transparently and systematically justify payment amounts using the worksheet. No special framework was needed; the framework proved extensible to the field's hardest case.

Source: Lynch, Darton, Levy, McCormick, Ogbogu, Payne, Roth, Shah, Smiley & Largent 2021, Am J Bioethics 21(3):11–31
Part 4 · Synthesis

The Big Picture — Everything, Connected

Cross-cutting themes, the complete concept inventory, and the study aids: glossary, self-check questions, and full source citations.

4.1  The argument of the week, in one page

Strip the five papers to their logical sequence and a single sustained argument emerges:

StepClaimAnchored byThe key move
1Human research on drugs (and infection) is scientifically necessary and ethically achievable under the Belmont principles.Stoops 2022Ethics is built into study design — consent, risk/benefit analysis, fair burden distribution — not appended to it.
2But paying participants for risk seems to compromise all of it — undue influence, commodification, exploitation of the poor.Wong & Bernstein 2011The classic objection: payment is a unique, certain benefit that biases consent; health shouldn't be a commodity.
3The objection conflates coercion with influence and treats payment as one undifferentiated lump. Fix the concepts and payment becomes analyzable.Gelinas et al. 2018Coercion = threat (payment can't be one); undue influence = inappropriate offers; itemize payment by function: reimbursement, compensation, incentive.
4In practice, paid participants don't experience payment as a clean trade — economic need shapes how they narrate harm itself.McManus et al. 2019Phase I volunteers minimize, deny, or re-attribute adverse events; the "safety" of trials is partly constructed by the people paid to endure them.
5Even at the extreme — deliberate infection with a deadly pathogen — the framework holds. What changes is the calibration, not the structure.Lynch et al. 2021No special framework for HICS; the payment funnel narrows from concepts to a worksheet with dollar amounts and benchmarks.
The thesis of the week

Payment is not a threat to research ethics that must be minimized — it is an instrument of research ethics that must be engineered. Unfairly low payment exploits; appropriately itemized payment respects; the ethical frontier is not "how little can we offer?" but "how do we justify what we offer, transparently, function by function?" The residual risks — distorted consent, deception, disproportionate burdens — are managed by safeguards around consent and comprehension, not by starving participants of fair compensation.

4.2  Cross-cutting themes

ThemeHow each paper treats it
Undue influence Wong: the central problem — payment's certainty biases any risk decision. Gelinas: defined precisely (an offer that causes unreasonable discounting of risk); distinguished from "mere" influence; managed with consent safeguards. Lynch: empirical evidence suggests it's smaller than feared (people weigh perceived risk first); incentives carry the highest potential but remain justifiable. McManus: the lived version — economic need shapes participants' very perception of harm.
Coercion vs. offer Gelinas: the definitional heart — coercion requires a threat; payment is an offer; only undue influence is ever at stake. Wong: concedes payment "may not strictly conform to the definition of coercion" but argues it's still a unique influence. This single distinction does enormous work in the debate.
Economic vulnerability Wong: the financially needy cross the risk threshold earlier (Figure 1) — so don't pay. Gelinas: paying less "because they are poor" exacerbates injustice; seek corrective measures. Lynch: exploitation can happen by paying too little, not only too much; site and participant selection must not target economic vulnerability; fair compensation is the priority. McManus: the empirical portrait — 84% of Phase I volunteers under $50k household income.
Informed consent Stoops: an ongoing process, threatened by blinding — mitigated by disclosure of possible drugs/doses and debriefing. Gelinas: safeguard consent directly (comprehension assessments) rather than restricting payment. McManus: consent's risk communication is undermined when participants deny that disclosed risks became actual harms. Lynch: consent supports for confinement (test confinement periods, prior-participant involvement); altruistic zeal needs the same protections money does.
Deception Gelinas: payment might induce eligibility deception — assess case by case. McManus: the documentation — participants suspected others of fabricating AEs to exit studies with full payment. Lynch: use objective enrollment criteria and adverse-event metrics; pay for anticipated median discomfort, not actual, to remove the incentive to exaggerate symptoms.
Compensation for harm Gelinas: better to compensate actual harms (insurance) than pay for risk; required as a matter of justice when harms materialize. Lynch: no-fault insurance is an absolute ethical requirement — an "ethical failing of the global research enterprise" that it isn't legally required; its own worksheet table (3B). Wong: the entire payment question is framed around harm probability. Stoops: the lab context — conservative dosing-termination criteria and medical infrastructure as harm prevention.
The wage/employment analogy Stoops: the wage-payment model in practice — matching the living wage, completion bonuses. Wong: the target of critique — wage models don't resolve commodification. Gelinas/Lynch: the foundation of the compensation category — equal pay for equal work, benchmarked to minimum wage and analogous occupations, never to individual opportunity cost.
Justice & diversity Stoops: open inclusion criteria, diverse recruitment, community partnership. Gelinas: fair distribution of risks and benefits. Lynch: HICS diversity is scientifically limited but burdens must not concentrate on the disadvantaged; reduce financial barriers rather than target groups with incentives.

4.3  Glossary of key terms

Adverse event (AE)
Any physiological sign, symptom, or medical event experienced by a participant during a trial, regardless of cause. Causation is adjudicated only after the trial — AEs are the raw material of Phase I safety testing (McManus et al. 2019).
Belmont Report
The 1979 foundational U.S. bioethics document articulating three principles — beneficence, respect for persons, justice — that undergird the federal regulations (cited by Gelinas; applied throughout Stoops).
Break point
In a progressive-ratio self-administration schedule, the highest response requirement a subject will complete for a drug dose — an index of reinforcing efficacy (Stoops 2022).
Coercion
A threat to harm someone or violate their rights. By definition, an offer of payment cannot coerce — the distinction on which the modern framework turns (Gelinas et al. 2018, following Wertheimer and the Belmont Report).
Completion bonus
A payment made only to participants who finish a study, used to minimize early withdrawal — acceptable when needed, but limited to studies offering fair reimbursement and compensation (Lynch et al. 2021; also Stoops's lab practice).
Drug discrimination
A behavioral procedure measuring a drug's discriminative stimulus effects: subjects trained on Drug A allocate points between "Drug A" and "Not Drug A"; the outcome is percent drug-appropriate responding (Stoops 2022).
Double-dummy design
A blinding strategy in which placebo versions of every active treatment are administered so neither subjects nor staff can identify conditions — used when multiple routes or dosing times are involved (Stoops 2022).
Human infection challenge study (HICS)
A study that deliberately infects healthy participants with a pathogen (e.g., SARS-CoV-2) to test vaccines, therapies, or host–pathogen questions under controlled conditions (Lynch et al. 2021).
Incentive
Payment beyond what fair reimbursement and compensation justify, offered to improve recruitment and retention; the most controversial payment category, but legitimate in principle (Gelinas et al. 2018).
Minimal risk
The regulatory standard (45 CFR 46.102(i)) framing research risk relative to the risks of daily life — an assumption McManus et al. problematize, since "daily life" is not a self-evident metric.
No-fault insurance
Guaranteed coverage of research-related harms — medical costs, lost wages, pain and suffering, death — paid without requiring proof of wrongdoing; the ethical requirement Lynch et al. place at the base of the payment funnel.
Patient/healthy volunteer
The two recruitment populations in payment debates: patients (who may benefit medically) and healthy volunteers (paid principally for time, burden, and risk — the Phase I and HICS workforce).
Payment funnel
Lynch et al.'s metaphor for applying the payment framework: from the broad basic framework, through factors relevant to all clinical research, to HICS-specific factors, ending in study-specific dollar amounts (Table 1).
Phase I trial
First-in-human testing of an investigational drug's safety and tolerability in healthy volunteers — the setting where compensation is highest relative to later phases ($100–300/day) and AEs are the primary data.
Reimbursement
Payment restoring participants to their financial baseline for out-of-pocket expenses; entails no net benefit and therefore cannot be unduly influential (Gelinas et al. 2018).
Respect for persons
The Belmont principle requiring autonomy in research decisions and extra protections for those with limited autonomy — operationalized through informed consent and capacity assessment (Stoops 2022).
Self-administration
A behavioral procedure measuring willingness to take drugs: subjects sample a dose, then work to earn it again; the objective index of reinforcing effects (Stoops 2022).
Undue influence
An offer of something desirable that influences decision making inappropriately — when its attractiveness causes participants to unreasonably discount or fail to appreciate risks (Gelinas et al. 2018). The only payment-relevant concept in the regulatory vocabulary.
Wage-payment model
Treating research participation like employment — paying a wage proportional to time rather than a lump sum — proposed by Dickert & Grady, critiqued by Wong & Bernstein, and quietly realized in Stoops's living-wage practice and the framework's compensation benchmarks.

4.4  Self-check questions

Test yourself before the exam. Click each question to reveal the answer — drawn only from the five papers.

1. Why does Gelinas et al. say payment cannot be coercive — and what concept replaces coercion in payment analysis?
Coercion is defined as a threat to harm someone or violate their rights. Payment is an offer of something desirable — and by definition an offer is not a threat. Therefore only undue influence — an offer that influences decision-making inappropriately, causing participants to unreasonably discount or fail to appreciate risks — is ever at stake in payment analysis. This is why U.S. regulations tell IRBs to minimize "coercion and undue influence," but payment discussions need only concern the latter.
2. What are the three categories of the payment framework, the justification for each, and the ethical concern each raises?
Reimbursement — for out-of-pocket expenses; justified by restoring participants' financial baseline (fairness); raises no undue-influence concerns because it confers no net benefit — its concern is insufficiency. Compensation — for time, burden, and inconvenience; justified by the employment analogy (fair pay for contributions); may raise undue-influence concerns when it exceeds opportunity costs, but the framework holds these are outweighed by fairness with safeguards. Incentive — payment beyond fair reimbursement and compensation; justified by recruitment and retention needs; carries the highest potential for undue influence, managed with consent safeguards.
3. Reconstruct Wong & Bernstein's logical argument that payment unjustly influences the poor. What are its assumptions and its conclusion?
Two assumptions: (1) increased risk is associated with decreased willingness to participate; (2) more financial need is associated with increased willingness. Plotting these, the higher-need curve sits above the lower-need curve; if there is a willingness threshold above which people participate, those with more financial need cross it at higher levels of risk. Conclusion: payment leads to an unjust situation in which poorer patients are more likely to be influenced to participate in studies with potentially harmful risks — so a policy of not paying for more-than-minimal-risk research should be adopted.
4. In McManus et al., what are the three narrative strategies healthy volunteers use regarding adverse events? Give one example of each.
① AEs as insignificant — real but trivial (Alison's fevers vs. the "extreme" side effects on the consent form; Paolo's reasoning that participants are "still healthy"). ② AEs as imagined or fabricated — not real at all (Lindsay attributing her nausea to overthinking; Bruce's "it's all psychosomatic"; Travis suspecting others fake symptoms to leave early with full payment). ③ AEs as distressing but not drug-caused — real and painful but attributed to the environment, restrictions, or other participants' misconduct (Jennifer's back pain vs. "terrible hospital beds"; Steve's headaches from caffeine withdrawal; Everett's code-blue explanation via guessed rule-breaking). The common function: avoiding the conclusion that a drug-related harm occurred.
5. Why do Lynch et al. conclude HICS do not need a distinct payment framework? Name the four candidate reasons they consider and reject.
Public trust — the basic framework itself helps justify offers and respond to distrust; low payment could equally damage trust. Risk level — Phase 1 toxicity studies can be riskier, yet payment there is routine; risk bears on whether the research is ethical, not on how to analyze payment. Social value — the framework already incorporates recruitment/retention goals that social value amplifies. Susceptibility to financial influence — evidence shows healthy participants' decisions hinge on perceived risk, not payment; HICS-specific data replicate this, and payments appear resistible (most non-participants wouldn't join even if payment doubled). The ethical concerns about payment are the same in kind as for all clinical research — only the calibration differs.
6. What is the "payment funnel," and what are its stages?
The funnel organizes the path from ethical theory to a dollar figure: (1) the basic framework — itemize payment as reimbursement, compensation, and incentive (broad end); (2) factors relevant to all clinical research — direct medical benefit, early withdrawal/termination, study location, economic vulnerability, study budget, participant perspectives; (3) factors especially salient for HICS — isolation and confinement, anticipated discomfort, risk of lasting harm, participant motivations, plus diversity, stigma, and ethics review capacity; (4) the worksheet (Tables 3A/3B) — benchmarks and reflection producing a justifiable payment range. Each step narrows the assessment without ever yielding a single algorithmic answer.
7. How does Stoops's lab handle the tension between blinding and informed consent?
The consent document discloses the full list of drugs, drug combinations, and routes of administration that may be administered, along with known side effects, plus an advisory that on any given day subjects will not know which they are receiving. Subjects get adequate time to read and process, can discuss the study with the PI, and receive full debriefing after completion. Capacity to consent is verified (quizzes, teach-back, mental-status screening) — reflecting the principle that informed consent is an ongoing process, not a signature.
8. Why do Lynch et al. argue that low payment can be more ethically problematic than high payment?
Because people with limited financial opportunities can be exploited in two ways: by taking advantage of a willingness to engage in unreasonable activities for money, or by taking advantage of a willingness to accept less than is fairly owed for undertaking reasonable activities. Given substantial protections against the former (ethics review, safeguards), the potential for unfairness through insufficient compensation is of greater concern. Low payment also threatens adequate recruitment and retention — and underpowered or terminated trials expose participants to risk with limited offsetting social benefit. Withholding payment cannot fix unethical research, and when research is ethical, doing so raises additional ethical concerns.
9. What is compensation for harm, why is it separated from other payment, and what does fairness NOT require paying for?
Compensation for harm covers significant research-related injuries — through no-fault insurance covering medical costs, lost wages, pain and suffering, and death. It is paid only if harm materializes, so it is not a net benefit and raises no undue-influence concerns; it is separated from the payment worksheet (Table 3B vs. 3A) so it is never folded into expected total payment. Fairness does not demand that risk itself be compensated — assuming a risk that never materializes is not a loss — though risk-based payments may be permissible under other rationales.
10. How does McManus et al.'s findings complicate the informed-consent safeguard that the framework papers propose?
The framework's answer to undue influence is to strengthen consent — comprehension assessments, better risk communication. But McManus shows actual participants deny that disclosed risks translate into bodily harms: they witnessed AEs and narrated them as insignificant, imagined, or non-drug-caused. If participants systematically re-interpret bodily changes away from harm, then even perfect risk disclosure may not produce accurate risk understanding — and participants may under-report AEs, undermining the AE-monitoring that is Phase I research's core function. Hence the authors' proposal to return results (tell participants how their AEs were classified) to make consent meaningful for serial participants.
11. What historical episode does Stoops use to illustrate the societal benefit of human behavioral pharmacology — and why is it ethically significant?
Behavioral-pharmacological data showing that crack and powder cocaine are pharmacologically similar (both producing rapid, robust positive effects when smoked/injected respectively — Hatsukami & Fischman 1996) informed the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010, challenging racially biased sentencing minimums between the two forms of cocaine. It is ethically significant because it exemplifies the Belmont principle of beneficence at the societal level: research producing benefits that correct injustice — "development of policy based on science rather than supposition."
12. What is the "wage-payment model," and how do the five papers variously use, critique, or realize it?
The model (Dickert & Grady 1999) treats research participation like employment — paying a wage for time rather than a lump sum that might unduly influence the risk decision. Stoops realizes it in practice: matching payments to the living wage with completion bonuses. Wong & Bernstein critique it: wage models don't resolve commodification or unjust influence and aren't feasible to implement universally. Gelinas and Lynch absorb its logic into the compensation category: benchmark to minimum wage and analogous occupations, equal pay for equal work, never tied to individual opportunity costs — making the wage analogy the foundation of fair payment rather than a solution to be rejected.
